newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Axa/Sun life, millennium bug.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Axa/Sun life, millennium bug.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Last week Proteus highlighted the branding problem facing the UK's Sun Life Provincial and Axa Equity & Law following the announcement that the two companies are planning a 690m merger.
Industry sources now reveal that the two are considering marketing themselves under an entirely new brand.

The newly-combined insurer, which will be the third-largest life assurance and pension provider in the UK, is to use the Sun Life brand to market life products through intermediaries while its direct sales operation will be branded Axa.
But the company, a subsidiary of French Insurer Axa-UAP, will initially trade under the name Newco, and will replace this with a new group brand which could replace both Sun Life and Axa.

The insurer is to bring its marketing departments under one roof to maximise cost savings. It may appoint a group marketing director to oversee the rebranding. Rob Lee, general manager of marketing at Sun Life, and Mike Ramsey, general manager, marketing, at Axa Equity & Law, are expected to stay in their roles.

Also on the branding front, Royal & Sun Alliance is launching its first campaign for its new life assurance division. The national press campaign is designed to emphasise the benefits of an expanded range of mortgage protection products.

Perhaps more imaginative is the approach being taken by Australian Mutual Provident (AMP). It is raising an electronic sign 280m above Sydney's city centre announcing the number of days remaining before the Sydney 2000 Olympic games begin. The sign will rest on top of the AMP Tower in Market Street, Sydney, and will cost an estimated 2.5 million Australian dollars..
--oo0oo--
Legal experts have hit upon a ruling in the UK's Court of Appeal which may bolster the defences of insurers against claims from the computer millennium bug.
Many companies are expected to try and claim against insurance policies for the cost of reprogramming their systems to cope with the change from 1999 to 2000.
A number of insurers are preparing to respond to the threat by inserting clauses which exclude cover for losses caused by the bug when policies come up for renewal at the end of the year.

Such exclusions have not been tested, but a decision in the case of Yorkshire Water Services vs Sun Alliance last year, which ruled out an attempt to claim the cost of preventative work on a sewage works, may become a useful precedent.
London law firm Lovell White Durrant said the millennium issue would be affected by the case.

"The operation of an insured peril will not be imminent until 31 December 1999, and by then there will have been a number of years in which to correct the problem. Any insured company which has not done so by then will be deliberately, or at best recklessly, running the risk."
However with competition as fierce as it is at the moment, many insurers are concerned that if they introduce such clauses, buyers will simply go to another insurer who isn't introducing them.
The idea is fine in principal, but not necessarily easy to apply.
